item.research_question: Is the 'glacial phase' in triphenyl phosphite (TPP) a distinct liquid state (liquid 2) or a mixture of glass 1 and nano-crystals, and can the liquid–liquid transition (LLT) be proven to be reversible and first-order without interference from crystallization?
item.processing_route: Flash differential scanning calorimetry (Flash DSC) with heating/cooling rates of 10^3 K s^-1 (1,000 K s^-1); conventional DSC with rates of 5–10 K min^-1; annealing at 216 K for up to 600 min to form glacial phase (glass 2); special temperature protocol involving quenching to 173 K, heating to Trc, holding for 0.1 s, and re-cooling.
item.test_conditions: Heating rates of 10^3 K s^-1 (Flash DSC) and 1/12 K s^-1 (conventional DSC); annealing temperatures of 208–216 K; annealing times (tw) ranging from 0 to 4,500 min; temperature range 173 K to >300 K; N2 atmosphere.
key_findings: Ultra-high speed heating (10^3 K s^-1) successfully avoids crystallization, which occurs immediately at slower rates (e.g., 1/12 K s^-1) around 240 K.
The glacial phase prepared by annealing at 216 K for 600 min shows no glass 1 signal, confirming it is glass 2, not a mixture with glass 1.
The endothermic peak at ~250 K is attributed to the reverse LLT (liquid 2 to liquid 1) with a transition heat of ~30 J g^-1, comparable to the forward LLT heat of ~25–27 J g^-1.
For annealing above the spinodal temperature (Ta=216 K), two distinct glass transitions are observed, indicating nucleation-growth (NG) type LLT with coexisting liquid phases.
For annealing below the spinodal temperature (Ta=214 K), a single glass transition shifts continuously, indicating spinodal decomposition (SD) type LLT.
The reverse LLT occurs via an SD-type transformation with no incubation time (<0.1 s), starting immediately after the glass 2-to-liquid 2 transition gains mobility.
The stability limit of liquid 2 against liquid 1 (spinodal temperature) is estimated at ~235 K.
item.mechanism: The authors propose a two-order-parameter model where LLT is a gas–liquid-like transition of the fraction of locally favoured structures (S). The transition is first-order, characterized by the coexistence of two distinct liquid states (liquid 1 and liquid 2) with different densities and order parameters. The transition type (NG or SD) depends on whether the system is in a metastable or unstable state relative to the spinodal temperatures.
item.limitations: The glass 2-to-liquid 2 transition is difficult to separate from the reverse LLT because the system gains mobility and the reverse LLT initiates almost simultaneously. The spinodal temperature and stability limit are estimated indirectly and may vary with pressure.
item.future_work: The authors suggest their experimental method may be useful for isolating LLT from nano-crystallization in other systems like water. They propose that the critical pressure Pc exists where the two spinodal temperatures merge, and the critical temperature Tc should be located above 235 K.
quotes: We kinetically isolate the reverse liquid-liquid transition from glass transition and crystallization with a high heating rate of flash differential scanning calorimetry
The transition heat of the reverse LLT does not depend on the heating rate in the range of 500∼2,000 K s−1 and is almost constant within ±1%

This is the first unambiguous evidence not only for the reversibility and the first-order nature of LLT in molecular liquids but also for the fact that the transition is between two distinct liquid states
